briefOverview: Jesus teaches that God’s kingdom overturns human notions of fairness and status, then predicts his suffering and models servant leadership, concluding with a mercy-filled healing.
summary: Jesus tells a parable of a landowner who pays the same daily wage to workers hired at various times, provoking complaints from early hires; the landowner defends his generosity and asserts his right to do good, concluding with the reversal saying, “the last shall be first, and the first last.” Jesus then predicts in detail his impending betrayal, condemnation, delivery to the Gentiles, mockery, scourging, crucifixion, and resurrection on the third day. The mother of James and John asks that her sons sit at Jesus’ right and left in his kingdom; Jesus speaks of the “cup” and “baptism” of suffering they will share and clarifies that such honors are the Father’s to grant. He rebukes power-seeking by teaching that greatness in his community is service, grounding it in his own mission to serve and to give his life “a ransom for many.” Finally, outside Jericho, two blind men persistently cry out to the “Son of David”; Jesus has compassion, heals them, and they follow him.
externalContext: In first-century Palestine, day laborers often waited in village marketplaces to be hired; a denarius was a typical daily wage for manual labor under Roman economy. The “third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours” reflect daylight divisions roughly at 9 a.m., noon, 3 p.m., and 5 p.m. Appeals to sit at a ruler’s right and left evoke seats of honor in ancient royal courts. Jericho lay on a main route to Jerusalem; pilgrims commonly passed through during festival seasons. The title “Son of David” was a messianic designation signaling hope for a Davidic deliverer.
externalReferences: The closing maxim of the parable echoes the previous chapter’s saying, “many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first” (Matthew 19:30), and the phrase “many are called, but few chosen” parallels Matthew 22:14. This is the third major passion prediction in Matthew, complementing earlier ones in 16:21 and 17:22–23. Jesus’ teaching on servant leadership and giving his life “a ransom for many” parallels Mark 10:42–45; his “cup” of suffering resonates with his later prayer in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39) and with Old Testament imagery of a cup of wrath (Psalm 75:8; Jeremiah 25:15). The healing near Jericho parallels accounts in Mark 10:46–52 and Luke 18:35–43, where a blind beggar is healed as Jesus approaches Jerusalem.
practicalQuestions: Where do I resent God’s generosity toward others, and how might I celebrate it instead?
How do I define greatness—in terms of power and recognition, or humble service?
What “cup” of costly obedience am I willing to share for Jesus’ sake?
When rewards seem unequal, how can I trust God’s justice and goodness?
Do I persist in calling out to God despite social pressure to be silent?
uncertainAreas: The precise scope of “many are called, but few chosen” in verse 16—whether it applies only to the parable or more broadly—is debated. The identity of those destined for the seats at Jesus’ right and left remains unspecified. The theological nuance of “ransom for many” (e.g., substitutionary vs. representative) is not fully explained within the chapter.
